wealth.text:
Switzerland's wealth statistics show one of the starkest gaps anywhere between the average and the typical household. UBS's Global Wealth Report 2025 put Switzerland's mean wealth per adult at $910,382 (roughly CHF 734,000) — the highest of any country in the world, a position Switzerland has held for years. Median wealth per adult, however, was just $145,555, only good enough for eighth place globally (behind Luxembourg, Belgium and Australia among others) — a sign that Switzerland's famous average wealth is heavily skewed upward by a relatively small, very wealthy population rather than reflecting a uniformly rich middle, and that the real opportunity in this market is concentrated among a narrower band of very wealthy individuals and institutions.

On the institutional side, Switzerland's defining feature — discussed in full under Pensions — is the sheer scale of its funded occupational pension system (BVG/LPP), unusual among European neighbours for being genuinely pre-funded rather than pay-as-you-go. Total Swiss social insurance capital (spanning both the funded 2nd-pillar occupational system and reserves held for the state 1st pillar) was reported at CHF 1,265 billion; the identifiable, professionally-managed institutional base sums to roughly $1.17 trillion on a narrower basis. Switzerland's insurance sector adds a further $484.9bn (Life plus Non-life, see Insurance below), and the country is also one of the world's leading single-family-office hubs, discussed under Family offices.

sources.label: iamexpat.ch, Switzerland tops 2026 UBS Wealth Report with $910K per adult

pensions.text:
Switzerland runs a genuine three-pillar system, but its defining feature — unusual among European neighbours — is that the second pillar is properly funded rather than pay-as-you-go, making it one of the deepest genuinely-invested pension markets in Europe. The first pillar, AHV/AVS (Alters- und Hinterlassenenversicherung), is a state PAYG scheme providing a basic income floor. The second pillar, BVG/LPP (occupational pension), is mandatory for employees earning above CHF 22,680 a year (2025 threshold) and requires employers and employees to build a genuinely invested individual retirement account, subject to a legally-set minimum interest rate (1.25% for 2026, unchanged since 2024) and a minimum conversion rate (6.8% in 2026) that determines how accumulated capital converts into a pension at retirement — a hybrid model that sits somewhere between classic DB and DC, since individual accounts are invested collectively by a Pensionskasse but carry regulatory guarantees that blur the classic DB/DC distinction used elsewhere. A voluntary, tax-advantaged third pillar (Säule 3a/Pilier 3a) sits on top for individual retirement saving.

The funded second pillar's overall health is closely watched: pension funds without a state guarantee reported an average coverage ratio of 117.1% at the end of 2025, up from 114.7% at the end of 2024, and average investment returns of 3.76% in 2024 and 4.33% in 2025 — a materially healthier funding picture than the UK's or Germany's DB legacy books, reflecting decades of consistent, mandatory pre-funding, and a genuinely stable, well-capitalised client base for managers.

The identifiable institutional base shows this scale directly. DB Pension (Corp) is the largest pool at $597.6bn, spanning both dedicated single-employer pension funds (UBS AG's own fund, Roche, Migros, Swisscom) and large multi-employer collective foundations (ASGA Pensionkasse, and Stiftung Auffangeinrichtung BVG, the mandatory nationwide safety-net fund for employers without their own scheme). DB Pension (Govt) totals $466.7bn, led by the Swiss Federal Social Security Funds, BVK (the canton of Zurich's pension fund), PUBLICA (the federal government's own pension fund), a large Graubünden cantonal fund, and public-sector employers including Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) and Swiss Post. DC-style assets remain much smaller for now (DC Pension (Corp) $69.5bn, DC Pension (Govt) $31.5bn), representing a growth segment as Swiss occupational provision continues to evolve.

sources.label: Fidav SA, Swiss pension funds (LPP/BVG / 2nd pillar): performance, solidity and what businesses and workers need to know in 2026

insurance.text:
The Swiss Insurance Association (SIA/SVV) reports that Swiss private insurers invested CHF 526 billion in capital markets in 2024, with CHF 497.6 billion in capital investment assets on their balance sheets and roughly CHF 512 billion in underwriting reserves — making insurers a major institutional investor in the Swiss economy in their own right. That domestic total lines up closely with OECD-sourced figures for the sector: Life insurance at $306.9bn and Non-life insurance at $178.0bn, a combined $484.9bn, a good cross-check against SIA's own CHF figure given the two currencies have traded close to parity.

Switzerland's insurance market is also home to two of the world's largest reinsurance groups (Swiss Re and, historically, several major primary insurers with global reach such as Zurich Insurance Group), giving the sector an international weight well beyond what the domestic balance-sheet totals alone suggest, and a natural entry point for managers with global reinsurance-adjacent capability.

sources.label: SIA/SVV, Balance sheet and income statement for the 2024 insurance market
OECD, Asset allocation of insurance companies dataset (data-explorer.oecd.org)

charities.text:
Switzerland's charitable-giving sector is overseen not by a single regulator but by ZEWO, an independent certifying foundation that has awarded a donation quality seal since 1940 (under its current name since 1990). The Zewo seal is held by several hundred organisations at any time (roughly 500, based on available counts) and is estimated to influence around CHF 2.25 billion of Swiss charitable donations each year, covering 21 standards spanning ethics, governance, efficient use of funds, and transparent accounting and fundraising practices.

ZEWO's role is about donor trust and fundraising conduct rather than publishing sector-wide investment-asset statistics, so this population is best approached qualitatively for now. The much better-measured Swiss foundation sector, covered separately below, represents the more realistic institutional-mandate opportunity.

sources.label: Zewo, Your donation in good hands (official overview)

foundations.text:
Switzerland has one of the highest concentrations of charitable foundations per capita anywhere in the world — around six times more foundations per capita than the United States or Germany. The Swiss Foundation Report 2025 (its sixteenth edition, jointly published by the Center for Philanthropy Studies at the University of Basel, SwissFoundations and the Centre for Foundation Law at the University of Zurich) counted 13,984 charitable foundations active at the end of 2025, with around 325 newly established and 253 dissolved during the year. Total foundation assets are estimated at roughly CHF 160 billion (estimates vary between about CHF 100-160bn depending on definition and source), and the report's newer analysis suggests Swiss grant-making foundations distribute around CHF 6 billion a year for public benefit in total — roughly twice the figure previously assumed — of which foundations under direct federal supervision alone account for CHF 4.6 billion. This is a very large and still under-penetrated opportunity for institutional managers.

The identifiable, professionally-managed institutional base is extremely small next to that population — $0.08bn from a single reporting institution — the starkest gap identified across the European markets reviewed here, reflecting a pattern seen elsewhere: institutional asset-manager reporting only captures foundations large and professionalised enough to appear as identifiable asset owners, a tiny fraction of Switzerland's very large, very fragmented foundation population. For managers, this points toward a substantial, largely untapped market best pursued directly through the foundation associations named above rather than sized from institutional data alone.

sources.label: Fundraiso, Swiss grant-making foundations distribute around CHF 6 billion annually
SWI swissinfo.ch, Swiss charitable foundations continue to flourish

family_offices.text:
Switzerland, and Geneva and Zurich specifically, is one of the world's leading family office hubs, alongside London, New York and Singapore. According to FamilyOfficeHub.io's database (as of June 2026), Switzerland hosts 91 documented single family offices and 187 multi-family offices, with Zurich now home to more multi-family offices than any other city in Europe and Geneva the leading hub for international and French-speaking families specifically. Together, five cantons — Zurich, Zug, Schwyz, Geneva and Vaud — account for 82% of all participating single family offices identified. Swiss single family offices alone are estimated to oversee CHF 785 billion in combined assets, equivalent to more than 90% of Switzerland's GDP and roughly 30% higher than two years earlier — one of the largest and fastest-growing family office markets in the world.

The identifiable, named-reporter base captures only a small slice of that: of 60 firms tagged as single-family offices in Switzerland, 5 report a usable, internally-consistent AUM figure, for a combined $37.7bn — led by L'Arche Holding S.A. ($13.7bn), Spectrum Value Management Ltd. ($7.2bn), Muller Milch Management AG ($6.1bn), Kirkbi A.G. ($6.0bn, the Kirk Kristiansen family's holding company behind the LEGO Group) and Ledunfly S.A. ($4.7bn). Against the CHF 785bn external estimate above, this $37.7bn captures under 5% of Switzerland's true single-family-office capital — the largest gap identified across the markets reviewed here, and a clear illustration of how far a named-reporters-only floor sits below the real scale of this notoriously private asset-owner type. For managers, this points to a very substantial, largely relationship-driven opportunity that will not be found through public disclosure alone.

sources.label: finews.com, Swiss Single Family Offices: New Study Reveals Surprising Insights
familyofficehub.io, Family Offices in Switzerland: The Complete Guide

sovereign_wealth_funds.text: Switzerland has no sovereign wealth fund, and no distinct SWF exists in the country to target for mandate purposes. The closest institution in scale is the Swiss National Bank (SNB) itself, whose balance sheet totalled around CHF 800-845 billion in early 2025, of which roughly CHF 710-720 billion was foreign currency reserves (mainly foreign-currency bonds and equities) plus around CHF 134 billion in gold holdings (1,040 tonnes) as of early 2026. The SNB's sheer size leads to informal comparisons with sovereign wealth funds, and its reserves are actively invested across global bond and equity markets — but it is a central bank managing monetary policy and currency stability, not a state investment vehicle accumulating fiscal surpluses or resource revenue for future generations, so it does not meet even the loose definition of a SWF used elsewhere in this analysis, consistent with how central banks are treated across comparable markets (the Bank of England, for instance) — worth noting since the SNB is not a realistic target for conventional sovereign-fund business development despite its scale.

sources.label: Swiss National Bank, Why does the SNB hold billions worth of assets and how does it manage these assets?

ocio.text:
Switzerland's version of pooled or delegated institutional investment runs mainly through Anlagestiftungen (investment foundations) rather than the UK-style independent fiduciary manager. These are collective vehicles that let smaller and medium-sized Pensionskassen delegate investment implementation — and, for some providers, much of the surrounding administration too — while the pension fund's own board of trustees retains strategic responsibility. Swiss Life's Anlagestiftung alone provides collective investment and administration services to more than 400 pension funds; the Zurich Anlagestiftung is the largest bank-independent investment foundation in the country; and newer entrants such as AGAST (established by Allianz Global Investors) show the model is still attracting new providers and remains open to new entrants.

Globally, Cerulli estimates the OCIO/fiduciary management industry grew to more than $3.3 trillion in assets by the end of 2024, projecting growth to $5.6 trillion by the end of the decade — but, as with Germany and France, no dedicated Switzerland-specific OCIO market survey was identified, and the Anlagestiftung model's structure (a collective legal vehicle rather than a discretionary mandate to a single manager) makes direct comparison with the UK's fiduciary management market difficult in any case. For managers, the practical entry point into this market is via an Anlagestiftung structure rather than a UK-style direct fiduciary mandate.

sources.label: Swiss Life Asset Managers, Anlagestiftung (Investment Foundation)
Cerulli Associates, Nearly $1.3 Trillion Expected to Flow into OCIO Industry Through 2029
